pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Reversible Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 Properties & changes of materials):** Pupils should be taught to demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-4):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4] (reversible changes are the focus here).

- **Operational details:** The organising idea is that a REVERSIBLE change alters how a material looks or its state but produces NO NEW SUBSTANCE — you can get the original material back. The canonical reversible set: changes of state (melt–freeze, evaporate–condense), dissolving (recover by evaporation), and mixing separable materials (unmix by filtering/sieving/magnet). Teach by the do-and-UNDO pairing: every reversible change is shown together with the action that reverses it, and the child confirms the SAME material is back. Contrast sharply with irreversible changes (next node) where a new substance forms and cannot be undone. Reinforce conservation — the material persists through a reversible change. Watch the intuition that melting/dissolving 'uses up' or destroys the material.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Given a change, the child predicts whether it is reversible, states the action that would reverse it, and justifies by whether the original material can be recovered (no new substance made).
bestPractices: Pair every reversible change with the action that reverses it (do-and-undo) and confirm the SAME material returns.
Group the canonical reversible set — changes of state, dissolving, and mixing separable materials — under the single test 'no new substance made'.
Contrast directly with an irreversible change so the boundary is felt, not just stated.
Reinforce conservation: the material persists through the change even when it looks gone.
Have pupils predict reversibility and name the reversing action before testing.
keyRepresentations: A do-and-undo bench with forward and reverse controls per station
A greyed-out reverse control on an irreversible teaser (burnt toast)
commonMisconceptions: Melting or dissolving destroys or uses up the material.
All changes can be undone (over-generalising reversibility to burning/cooking).
A change of state makes a new substance rather than the same substance in a new state.
Mixing is irreversible because the materials 'became one thing'.
If a material looks different after a change, it must be a different material.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds learning that dissolving, mixing, and changes of state are reversible (no new substance is made and the original material can be recovered). The core method is do-and-undo: perform a change, perform the action that reverses it, and confirm the SAME material has returned. Contrast this with an irreversible change (e.g. toasting bread) where a new substance forms. Emphasise conservation — the material persists even when it looks gone — and have learners judge by 'was a new substance made?' rather than by appearance or by whether heat was involved.

activities.title: The do-it, undo-it bench
feedback: When the chilled chocolate sets again, confirm: 'Same chocolate back — melting and freezing just change the state, not the substance.'
If a learner expects the salt to be gone for good, point to the recovered crystals: 'It looked gone, but it was still there dissolved — evaporating brings it back.'

At the sand station, if a learner thinks the sand and water 'became one thing', show the filter re-separating them: 'Mixing separable materials is reversible — the sand and water were never combined into a new substance, so they come apart again.'

For the toast station, state: 'The reverse control is off because toasting made a new substance — appearance changing a lot (as in dissolving) is still reversible, but a new substance forming is not.'
After the round-trips, ask the learner to state the single test that worked for all three: 'Was a new substance made?'
activities.rationale: Pairing each change with its reversal and confirming recovery lets learners experience reversibility as a felt round-trip and directly targets the intuition that melting/dissolving destroys material. The greyed-out toast reverse control provides a within-task contrast so the reversible/irreversible boundary is experienced, not just stated. The forward/reverse controls and the 'same material recovered?' indicator are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms — the same learning can come from real melt/freeze, dissolve/evaporate, and filtering activities.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes
Children think melting/dissolving destroys or uses up material; pairing a change with its reversal and confirming recovery targets this
learnerActions: At station 1, gently warm a chunk of chocolate (e.g. in a bowl over warm water) only until it flows, then chill it and confirm it sets back into solid chocolate. Overheated chocolate can scorch or burn, which makes new substances and cannot be undone.
At station 2, stir salt into water until it seems to disappear (it is still there, dissolved), then gently heat the dish and confirm salt crystals reappear.

At station 3, tip sand into water, pour the mixture through a filter, and confirm the sand is separated out on the filter (damp, but the same sand) while the water passes through (it may be slightly cloudy if the sand has very fine particles).

For each station, do the change and then the reversing action, and check whether the same material has been recovered before moving on (if using a screen or bench simulation, this may be a forward/reverse control and a 'same material recovered?' indicator).

At a fourth station, an adult toasts a slice of bread; try to think of any action that would turn it back into bread and notice there is none ('you can't un-toast it — a new substance was made'). In a simulation, this may appear as a greyed-out reverse control.
Before testing each station, predict whether the change is reversible and say out loud the action that would reverse it.
activities.intendedInsight: A reversible change alters how a material looks or its state but makes NO new substance, so you can get the original material back by undoing it; some changes (toasting) make a new substance and cannot be undone.

activities.title: Reverse-arrow summary chart
feedback: If a learner pairs dissolve with the wrong recovery, remind them: 'Evaporating the water leaves the solid behind.'
Reinforce that all three pairs pass the same test, so the category is organised by substance, not by appearance.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or arrow-pairing chart organises the category clearly and consolidates the vocabulary after hands-on work. It is a summary companion: on its own it does not let the learner perform the round-trip and verify recovery, so it works best after the bench or real experiments rather than instead of them.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes
learnerActions: Match each change to its reversing action: melt⇄freeze, dissolve⇄evaporate, mix⇄filter.
Reveal or state what gets you back to the original material for each pair.
Add the single test that unites all three pairs: 'no new substance made'.
activities.intendedInsight: The canonical reversible changes — changes of state, dissolving, and mixing separable materials — all share one test: no new substance is formed, so the original can be recovered.

activities.title: Sort and justify: reversible or not?
feedback: If a learner calls dissolving irreversible because the solution looks different, respond: 'Appearance changed, but evaporating recovers the solid, so it is reversible — judge by substance, not looks.'
If a learner calls melting irreversible because heat was used, line it up against toasting: 'Both used heat; only toasting made a new substance.'
Reward justifications that name the recovery action and the 'no new substance' test rather than just the label.
activities.rationale: The learning target here is a sorting-plus-justification judgement, so a categorise-and-match-with-reasons task is a genuinely apt format. Because recognition and matching do not by themselves require the learner to perform and observe the round-trip, pair this with the bench or real experiments so judgements rest on experienced recovery rather than guessing.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes
NGSS 2-PS1-4: construct an argument that some heating/cooling changes can be reversed and some cannot
learnerActions: Categorise a set of changes as reversible or irreversible.
Match each reversible change to the specific action that would reverse it.
For each judgement, state the reason: can the original material be recovered, with no new substance made?
Tackle tricky cases: is dissolving salt reversible even though the water looks completely different? Is re-set chocolate the same substance?
activities.intendedInsight: Reversibility is judged by whether a new substance was made and the original can be recovered — not by whether heat was added or whether the material looks different.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain with chocolate
feedback: If a learner predicts 'no' because heating spoils it, contrast melting ice (heated, reversible) with toasting (heated, irreversible) to move them off 'heat' and onto 'was a new substance made?'.
If a learner judges by appearance, use dissolving as the bridge: it looks totally different yet is reversible by evaporation.
Confirm a strong answer: ice↔water is reversible (same water, just a change of state); bread→toast is irreversible (a new substance forms).
activities.rationale: Eliciting the reason before observing is diagnostic because heat is present in both the melting and toasting examples, so a learner reasoning from 'heating = irreversible' gets the reason wrong even when the label is right. This separates classification by 'same substance / no new material' from classification by surface cues.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-4: construct an argument that some heating/cooling changes can be reversed and some cannot
Children think melting/dissolving destroys or uses up material; pairing a change with its reversal and confirming recovery targets this
learnerActions: Before any melting, predict: if we melt this chocolate in a bowl and then put it in the fridge, will we get chocolate back — and WHY?
State your reason out loud before observing (this reasoning is the important part).
Melt the chocolate, then let it set, and compare your prediction with what happened.

Answer probe questions: Is dissolving salt reversible even though it looks nothing like before? Would un-heating toast make it bread again, and why not? Then give your own test for 'reversible' that works no matter what the change looks like.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating the reason before observing surfaces whether a learner is reasoning from 'heating spoils it' or appearance versus the correct test of whether a new substance was made.

constraints: Use real melt/freeze, dissolve/evaporate, and filter activities as the ideal hands-on experience; screen or bench simulations are a scaffold that can preview the round-trip but should not replace acting on real materials and confirming recovery.
The summary chart and sorting/matching tasks consolidate and assess the category; on their own they do not require the learner to perform and observe recovery, so pair them with doing the changes.
Keep the focus on reversible changes as specified, but use one irreversible example (toasting) only as a contrast — do not let it become the main lesson of this node.
Heating is involved in both a reversible example (melting) and an irreversible one (toasting); never teach 'heat makes a change irreversible'. The deciding test is whether a new substance was made.
Supervise heating of chocolate, heating of salt solution, and use of the grill; these involve hot surfaces and should be adult-led or closely supervised for this age group.
Illustrative interface details (forward/reverse controls, 'same material recovered?' indicator, greyed-out reverse button) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.

Recovered material is the same substance even when its physical form differs (damp rather than dry sand, salt returning as crystals); keep learners focused on 'same substance', not identical appearance.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated conversation and 3D as poor fit with universal-sounding reasons ('3D adds cost without insight', dialogue 'cannot produce that evidence'). These have been reframed as scope-limited: those formats are less suited to producing recovery evidence for this specific target, not proven incapable. Comparative efficacy and necessity are not established by the source claims provided.

One source (RSC misconceptions guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; the claim about children thinking melting/dissolving destroys material is retained where it directly supports the teaching principle but is treated as unverified legacy content with no fresh verification asserted.

The original recommendation described 'dry sand' after filtering; filtered sand is actually damp. This was corrected to 'damp, same sand' so the point remains recovery of the same substance, not dryness.

Scientific note for review: salt recovered by evaporation returns as crystals that may differ in form from the original grains, and re-set chocolate may differ in texture; the substance is the same, which is the point. If learners notice such differences, clarify that reversibility concerns the substance, not the exact appearance.
The row cites NGSS 2-PS1-4, a grade-2 standard, for a 9–10 age node; retained from the original row and not treated as a learner-facing error.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: hold up a bar of chocolate. Ask the child to predict — if we melt it in a bowl and then put it in the fridge, will we get chocolate back, and WHY? A child anchored on 'heating spoils it' predicts no. Melt and re-set it. It's chocolate again (reversible). The stated reason before observing is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Dissolving salt in water — reversible or not? It looks nothing like before. How do you decide?
You melted a chocolate bar and let it set again. Same substance or new one? Reversible?
What if the toast could be un-heated back to room temperature — would that make it bread again? Why not?
Give me your own test for 'reversible' that works no matter what the change looks like.
assess.correctAnswer: Ice↔water is REVERSIBLE: melting and freezing just change the state; it's the same water, no new substance is made, so you can get the ice back by cooling. Bread→toast is IRREVERSIBLE: a new substance forms (you can't turn toast back into soft bread). The 'why' is the key: reversible changes make NO new material, so the change can run backwards.

errorPatterns.pattern: any change caused by heating is irreversible ('you heated it, so it can't go back')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up melting ice (heated, reversible) against toasting (heated, irreversible) — force the child off 'heat' and onto 'was a new substance made?'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ice melting can't be undone because you had to heat it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls melting irreversible because heat was involved, or can't say why toast differs from melted ice when both used heat

errorPatterns.pattern: reversible means 'looks the same afterwards' rather than 'same substance, no new material'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use dissolving as the bridge: it looks totally different yet is reversible (evaporate to recover). Reversibility is about substance, not looks.
errorPatterns.distractor: Dissolving salt is irreversible because the water looks completely different now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: judges by appearance — calls dissolving irreversible because the solution looks different, though the solid is recoverable

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by surface cue (heat added, looks different); labels may be right but reasons are wrong, or can't say why one undoes and one doesn't.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by 'same substance / no new material made', explains why heat isn't the deciding factor, and transfers the rule correctly to dissolving and melting-then-setting — reversibility judged by substance, not appearance.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly labels the two examples and says 'no new substance' for reversible, but can't yet apply it to a tricky case (dissolving, re-set chocolate) — the rule is stated, not yet transferable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Think of ice melting into water, and water freezing back into ice. Now think of a slice of bread turning into toast under the grill. One of these can be undone to get exactly what you started with, and one can't. Which is which — and, the important part, WHY can you undo one but not the other?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who classifies by 'no new substance / same stuff in a new form' from one who classifies by surface cues like 'you added heat' or 'it looks different'. Heat is present in BOTH examples, so a child reasoning from 'heating = irreversible' gets the reason wrong even if the label is right.
